extracted.intended_audience: American statesmen, informed citizens, and readers interested in constitutional design and political philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: A short, comparative analysis of republican and monarchical constitutions identifying principles that make republics 'free' or prone to degeneration (separation of powers, checks and balances, representation, safeguards against corruption and foreign influence). Intended to guide judgment about constitutional design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers
rubrics_metrics.description: A distinct separation of the legislative from the executive power, and of the judicial from both — the text notes this is rare except in England and praises the United States for careful separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that without distinct separation the government will become either an absolute monarchy or an oligarchy. Praise is given to systems (England, United States) that carefully separate legislative, executive, and judicial powers as necessary to enable 'the laws alone' to govern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilibrium of the three estates (the one, the few, and the many)
rubrics_metrics.description: Power should be balanced among the one (chief magistrate), the few (senate/oligarchy), and the many (popular assembly) to prevent any single order from dominating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly asserts that a 'balance' or 'equilibrium' of powers is an 'eternal rule in politics' and that failure to maintain such balance leads to tyranny, absolute monarchy, or an arrogant nobility which annihilates the people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict execution of the laws (rule of law)
rubrics_metrics.description: A free republican government 'consists in a strict execution of its laws' — laws must be executed firmly and impartially for government to function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts mere names (a constitution called 'republic') with real governmental substance: laws must govern through consistent, strict execution. Lack of execution leads to disorder and degeneration of republican institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and frequent elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemblies (representatives, senators, governors) should be chosen regularly and frequently; representation must be proportionate and adequate to be 'the most equitable' form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Americans are commended for annual selection of representatives, senators, and governors; the author notes that frequent elections and popular participation secure the people's share of power and prevent aristocratic capture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate confined to legislative power (limitation of senatorial executive power)
rubrics_metrics.description: Senates should be debarred from executive power and confined to the legislative role to avoid aristocratical ambition and oligarchy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When senates share executive power they tend to 'produce...ardent aristocratical ambition' and end in oligarchy; where confined to legislative power they 'have been observed to be firm barriers against the encroachments of the crown.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a chief magistrate (a head)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every polity has, and needs, a principal personage — stadtholder, doge, president, governor, or king; the body politic cannot subsist without a head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author rejects the notion that a republic should have no chief; governors are defended as necessary and not singularly blameworthy (e.g., Americans are not justly censured for instituting governors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial by jury
rubrics_metrics.description: Trial by jury preserved in its full vigor is a characteristic of a free republic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author lists trials by jury among the chief protections of liberty and connects it to the general claim that where such circumstances exist, 'the laws alone can govern.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of a standing army
rubrics_metrics.description: A free republic should avoid a standing army; lack of a standing army is presented as a civil liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: England is praised for curbing the nobility 'without giving him a standing army.' The presence of a standing army is implied to threaten liberty and the people's supremacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habeas corpus
rubrics_metrics.description: The habeas corpus should be in full force as a protection of personal liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Habeas corpus is cited among key institutional protections alongside jury trial and separation of powers; it underpins protection from arbitrary detention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free press
rubrics_metrics.description: A free press is a central element of liberty and of a free republic ('the press is the most free in the world').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom of the press is listed with other liberties that enable laws and public opinion to check power; it contributes to accountability and public information.

rubrics_metrics.name: No hereditary titles, honours, offices, or distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Out-of-office all men should be of the same 'species'; society should avoid hereditary ranks that entrench unequal orders of men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author celebrates America for lacking hereditary distinctions and sees this equality (outside office) as contributing to republican virtue and preventing entrenched aristocracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security of property
rubrics_metrics.description: The property of subjects must be secured; protection of property is a mark of a tolerable constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the account of Poland property security is linked to a tolerable constitution; loss of protection and increasing noble power correlate with peasant poverty and civic decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of unanimity veto (liberum veto) and requirements for unanimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules requiring unanimity or allowing single-member vetoes (the liberum veto) produce paralysis, faction, foreign manipulation, and effectively leave a country 'above a hundred years almost without laws.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poland's liberum veto is given as a concrete anti-pattern: a single nuncio's 'I stop the proceedings' could break diets, be bought by foreign powers, and led to legislative paralysis and eventual partition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards against foreign influence and venal elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions must prevent foreign powers and venality from determining internal outcomes (e.g., bribery of nobles, foreign troops at elections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recounts Polish elections secured by bribery and foreign troop deployments (e.g., five thousand Russian troops at an election) and argues such practices fatally undermine liberty and independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular convening of representative assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative assemblies should be required to meet regularly (example: diets assembled every two years in Poland's pacta conventa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular convocation prevents extended executive or oligarchic dominance and ensures ongoing representation and accountability; irregular or king-controlled convocation can enable abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional limits on monarch's fiscal and legislative powers
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental laws limiting a monarch (e.g., 'The king cannot impose taxes; cannot alienate the royal domains; cannot enact laws; cannot coin money; cannot alter process in courts') are required to restrain executive overreach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text cites Alexander's 1505 limitations as examples of charters of immunities (pacta conventa). Such enumerated prohibitions aim to protect the polity from arbitrary monarchical power but may be undermined in practice by other weaknesses (e.g., bribery, venality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent and consistent judicial process
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial processes and appellate structures should be secure and not manipulable by partisan authorities; the king should not be able to alter court procedure at will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poland's removal of supreme jurisdiction and the establishment of palatinate-elected judges (tribunalia regni) that decide nobles' causes without appeal illustrates that decentralised or partisan judicial arrangements can remove checks and produce impunity; consistent processes and appealability are implied as necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control over patronage and appointments with checks
rubrics_metrics.description: The appointive power (bestowing offices, fiefs, dignities) must be balanced; unchecked patronage preserves influence but can be wrested away and abused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The king's power to bestow royal fiefs made him 'the fountain of honour' and preserved influence; later creation of permanent councils and distribution of offices to life-tenure office holders who were 'responsible only to the diets' produced avenues for abuse and evasion of inquiry.
